text: With identity federated and the fleet hardened, Castellan runs its first joint access certification campaign, covering both the legacy finance team and the newly onboarded claims-payment staff together — and it surfaces something that had existed, undetected, since before the merger even started.

Senior claims analyst Dana Whitfield holds both the Claims Adjuster role, which can create and approve claim payment requests, and the Payment Approver role, which approves the wire transfers that actually pay them out. Held together, one person can originate a claim and approve its own disbursement, with no second set of eyes at any point.

The combination is fourteen months old. A colleague on the claims-payment team went on extended leave, Dana got temporary approval coverage, the colleague came back, and the grant was simply never removed afterward. Thornbury's role catalog never encoded these two roles as mutually exclusive, and no separation-of-duties check ever ran against it. A human reviewer noticing one report line is what finally caught it.

The Payment Approver role carries a fifty-thousand-dollar transaction limit, which sets the real exposure across those fourteen months. The investigation pulls roughly two hundred thirty claims Dana originated in that window and cross-checks every approval. Zero were self-approved. The gap was real and the exposure was real, but no fraud actually occurred.

The fix has two parts. Immediately, Payment Approver is revoked from Dana's account — she keeps Claims Adjuster, her actual job — and an uninvolved backup approver is assigned. The slower, structural part writes a separation-of-duties check as code, run nightly against the role-assignment table, so the next toxic combination gets flagged automatically instead of waiting a year for someone to notice by chance.

The mutual-exclusion rule also gets added directly to the formal role catalog itself, so provisioning tooling rejects the combination at assignment time, before it's ever granted. Next up: the final lesson, tying identity architecture, authentication, authorization, hardening, and governance together into one closing capstone review.
